params.question: The crystalline lens contributes more refracting power than the cornea because it can change shape through accommodation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, the cornea provides approximately 43 dioptres — about two-thirds of the eye's total refracting power — while the lens adds only 17 to 20 dioptres. The lens's ability to change shape through accommodation makes it adjustable, but the cornea remains the dominant refractive element.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! The cornea actually provides the larger share — approximately 43 dioptres of the eye's total 60 dioptres — while the lens adds only 17 to 20 dioptres. Accommodation makes the lens adjustable, not more powerful. The cornea's fixed power accounts for roughly two-thirds of total refraction.

interactions.label: A young patient with hypermetropia has normal distance vision but reports fronta

params.question: A young patient with hypermetropia has normal distance vision but reports frontal headaches after prolonged reading. Which mechanism explains the absence of distance blur?

answers.text: Hypermetropia causes blur only at near distances, so distance vision is inherently unaffected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hypermetropia affects all distances — the focal point falls behind the retina whether the object is near or far. The absence of distance blur is due to active compensation by the crystalline lens, not a selective effect.

answers.text: The young eye uses accommodation to bring the focal point forward onto the retina, compensating for the error

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The young hypermetropic eye accommodates continuously — the ciliary muscle contracts to increase lens power, shifting the focal point forward onto the retina. Prolonged near work demands even more accommodation, producing strain and headaches.

answers.text: The cornea temporarily steepens during distance viewing to increase its refractive power

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The cornea does not change shape dynamically — its 43 dioptres of power are fixed. The compensation comes from the crystalline lens adjusting through ciliary muscle contraction.

answers.text: Tear film irregularity selectively reduces near acuity while sparing distance vision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Tear film issues cause fluctuating blur at all distances, not the specific pattern of clear distance vision with near-work headaches. The mechanism here is the extra accommodative effort the lens must make.

overallFeedback.feedback: In hypermetropia, the focal point falls behind the retina. Young eyes compensate by accommodating — the ciliary muscle contracts to increase lens power and shift focus forward. This continuous effort is tolerable for distance but causes symptoms during prolonged near work.

Correct! Accommodation masks the hypermetropic error at distance, but sustained near work demands additional effort from the ciliary muscle, producing the characteristic frontal headaches and eye strain.

interactions.label: A 50-year-old patient presents with visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. With

params.question: A 50-year-old patient presents with visual acuity of 6/24 in the right eye. With a pinhole disc, acuity does not improve. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Prescribe concave spectacle lenses for presumed myopia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The pinhole did not improve acuity, which means the cause is not refractive. Spectacles correct optical errors only — they cannot compensate for retinal or optic nerve damage.

answers.text: Perform cycloplegic refraction to unmask hidden hypermetropia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Cycloplegic refraction is useful when accommodation masks a refractive error, typically in younger patients. When the pinhole fails to improve acuity, the problem lies beyond refraction entirely.

answers.text: Repeat the test with the other eye occluded to confirm the reading

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Each eye should be tested separately as standard technique, but the key finding — no pinhole improvement — already provides the critical diagnostic information and does not change on repetition.

answers.text: Refer for evaluation of cataract, optic nerve, or macular pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! No pinhole improvement indicates organic pathology — cataract, optic nerve disease, or macular damage. These conditions require specialist evaluation and cannot be corrected by spectacles or refraction.

overallFeedback.feedback: When the pinhole fails to improve acuity, the cause is organic — cataract, macular disease, or optic nerve pathology — not a refractive error. No spectacle correction can help; specialist referral is needed.

Correct! The pinhole test is a rapid screen at the bedside: improvement points to a refractive cause correctable with spectacles, while no improvement signals organic disease requiring urgent referral.

interactions.label: A 22-year-old with stable −4 D myopia requests LASIK. Pre-operative corneal topo

params.question: A 22-year-old with stable −4 D myopia requests LASIK. Pre-operative corneal topography reveals subclinical keratoconus, though slit-lamp examination appears normal. What is the most appropriate decision?

answers.text: Proceed with LASIK since the refraction is within treatable range and slit-lamp findings are normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A normal slit-lamp cannot rule out keratoconus — topography is the definitive screening tool. The topographic finding overrides clinical appearance and identifies a structurally compromised cornea.

answers.text: Switch to PRK, which avoids creating a flap and is biomechanically safer for this cornea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although PRK avoids a flap, any excimer laser ablation on a keratoconic cornea further weakens it. The risk of progressive post-operative ectasia applies to all corneal laser procedures.

answers.text: Decline all corneal laser procedures — subclinical keratoconus is an absolute contraindication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Subclinical keratoconus absolutely contraindicates all corneal laser procedures — LASIK, PRK, and SMILE alike. Operating on a structurally compromised cornea risks progressive ectasia regardless of the technique.

answers.text: Proceed with a reduced ablation depth to preserve a thicker residual stromal bed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Reducing ablation depth does not address the fundamental problem: the cornea is biomechanically unsound. No depth adjustment makes ablation safe on a keratoconic cornea.

overallFeedback.feedback: Subclinical keratoconus, detectable only on topography, absolutely contraindicates LASIK, PRK, and SMILE. Operating on such a cornea makes post-operative ectasia nearly inevitable, regardless of technique or ablation parameters.

Correct! Topographic keratoconus — even subclinical — is an absolute contraindication to corneal laser surgery. Rigorous pre-operative screening is what prevents the catastrophic complication of post-operative ectasia.

interactions.label: A 5-year-old child reads 6/6 with isolated single letters but only 6/18 on the s

params.question: A 5-year-old child reads 6/6 with isolated single letters but only 6/18 on the standard Snellen line chart in the right eye. The left eye scores 6/6 on both. What does this discrepancy most likely indicate?

answers.text: An uncorrected refractive error in the right eye requiring spectacle correction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. An uncorrected refractive error reduces acuity equally on single letters and full lines. The selective drop on the line chart with preserved single-letter acuity points to a cortical processing deficit, not an optical one.

answers.text: Poor cooperation from the child, requiring retesting at a later visit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Inconsistent cooperation produces random errors, not a systematic pattern of worse line acuity with preserved single-letter acuity. This reproducible pattern is the crowding phenomenon.

answers.text: Amblyopia in the right eye, demonstrated by the crowding phenomenon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The crowding phenomenon — worse acuity on a line chart than with isolated letters — is virtually diagnostic of amblyopia. Surrounding contours interfere with letter recognition in the amblyopic visual cortex.

answers.text: A testing artefact from improper chart distance that affects line reading more than single letters

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Chart distance affects all measurements equally in both eyes. The inter-eye difference combined with the specific single-letter versus line-chart discrepancy points to the crowding effect in amblyopia.

overallFeedback.feedback: Better single-letter acuity than line-chart acuity in one eye is the crowding phenomenon, virtually diagnostic of amblyopia. It reflects cortical processing difficulty in the amblyopic eye, not an optical or cooperation problem.

Correct! The crowding phenomenon is a hallmark of amblyopia — the amblyopic cortex struggles to resolve a letter when flanked by others, causing line-chart acuity to fall well below single-letter acuity.
